overview: Five documents trace the Japanese government's campaign from 1934 to 1936 to consolidate the rival Rengo Tsushin and Nippon Dempo news services into the state-favored Domei Tsushinsha, followed by a 1939 memorandum alleging that Domei was distributing fabricated reports abroad. Embassy despatches describe the financial and institutional mechanisms of consolidation, including Japan Broadcasting Company funding, government subsidies, preferential communications facilities, pressure upon newspapers, and a planned Cabinet information committee. Taken together, the file documents the replacement of competitive news gathering by a centralized system intended to shape domestic opinion, promote an officially approved image of Japan overseas, and reduce foreign influence.

subfiles.title: Despatch on the proposed amalgamation of Rengo and Nippon Dempo
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, U.S. Ambassador to Japan
subfiles.about: Reports government-backed negotiations to consolidate Japan's two leading news agencies as a means of tightening official control over domestic and international news.
subfiles.summary: Grew reports that the Japanese government is pressing Rengo Tsushin and Nippon Dempo Tsushin, respectively linked to the Associated Press and United Press, to amalgamate. Although officially justified by economy and reduced competition, the plan is described as part of preparations for the anticipated “crisis of 1935-36” and an effort to ensure that only an approved Japanese viewpoint circulates at home and abroad. Financial demands, newspaper resistance, leadership appointments, and the future of the agencies' foreign contracts remain unresolved.

subfiles.title: Despatch on Japan Broadcasting Company participation in the agency merger
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, U.S. Ambassador to Japan
subfiles.about: Explains a revised consolidation plan under which the Japan Broadcasting Company would finance the liquidation of the existing news agencies and join their successor.
subfiles.summary: The Embassy reports that the proposed amalgamation has been expanded to include the Japan Broadcasting Company because the press refused a direct government loan or subsidy and lacked the capital to acquire Nippon Dempo. The broadcaster would use its accumulated reserves to finance the liquidation of the existing agencies and hold a mortgage or lien over their assets until repaid. Although formally a nonprofit association, the company monopolized Japanese radio broadcasting and operated under the general control of the Minister of Communications.

subfiles.title: Despatch on the establishment of Domei Tsushinsha
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, U.S. Ambassador to Japan
subfiles.about: Describes the organization, financing, political purpose, and competitive strategy of the new Domei Tsushinsha.
subfiles.summary: Domei Tsushinsha held its inaugural meeting on December 17, 1935, and planned to begin operations on January 1, 1936, under Tokichi Tanaka and Eisuke Fukuda. The Embassy regarded it as a strengthened and renamed Rengo, financed substantially by the Japan Broadcasting Company and designed to compel the unsubsidized Nippon Dempo to sell. Benjamin W. Fleisher warned that Nippon Dempo's disappearance would deprive the Japan Advertiser of an affordable, independent source of foreign news. The despatch also records military dissatisfaction that Domei was not sufficiently national or governmental, an ultimatum to Nippon Dempo, and the broader objective of unifying news services under government auspices.

subfiles.title: Despatch confirming the merger of Domei and Nippon Dempo
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, U.S. Ambassador to Japan
subfiles.about: Reports Nippon Dempo's agreement to merge with Domei and reproduces the Japanese government's public rationale for a unified national news agency.
subfiles.summary: Communications Minister Keikichi Tanomogi announced that Nippon Dempo had agreed to amalgamate with Domei, with the new combined organization expected to emerge around May 1, 1936. His statement presented unification as necessary for authoritative reporting, sound public opinion, international understanding of Japan, execution of national policy, and world peace. Grew instead characterizes the merger as a means of placing news under strict government control and disseminating an officially approved patriotic viewpoint. The despatch also notes plans for a Cabinet information committee representing the principal ministries concerned with foreign policy, the armed forces, communications, and domestic affairs.

subfiles.title: Hornbeck memorandum on fabricated Domei news
subfiles.from: Stanley K. Hornbeck, Adviser on Political Relations
subfiles.about: Records Hornbeck's warning to the British Ambassador that Domei was intensively circulating fabricated reports about American and British policy.
subfiles.summary: Hornbeck told Lord Lothian that Domei reports from several parts of the world contained unfounded statements about U.S. policy and statements known to be false about other governments. He cited a London report claiming that Britain had abandoned its former Far Eastern policy and was helping Japan break Chinese resistance and impose a Japanese peace upon China. Lothian said that he had noticed the proliferation of Domei material in the American press and would inform his government of the specific report.

interest: The file offers an unusually coherent chronological record of how a nominally voluntary news-agency merger became an instrument of Japanese information policy. It is especially useful for connecting financial arrangements, subsidies, communications privileges, newspaper economics, and bureaucratic coordination to the growth of state control over news. The final 1939 memorandum provides a revealing outcome: within a few years, U.S. officials viewed the consolidated agency not merely as controlled media but as an international distributor of fabricated geopolitical reporting.
